activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: A conclusion restates the thesis in fresh words and sums up the main points, but it should not introduce a brand-new argument.
story:
Claire had one goal by Friday: convince her whole class to boycott the cafeteria. It had started when she found a patch of grey fungus on her hamburger bun, and she had taken a photo of it before anyone could throw the evidence away. Now she had three arguments lined up, a systematic plan for her five paragraphs, and a spot on Ms. Li's list to read her draft aloud.

She read the first four paragraphs to Arie and Benson at lunch, and even Benson, who normally argued with her about everything, nodded along. Then she reached the last paragraph and slowed down, because it was her favourite part. "In conclusion, if we boycott the cafeteria, the school will have to cancel the spring dance too, since the same company runs both." She looked up. "That's my best idea, right?"

Arie frowned at the paper. "Wait. Why didn't you say that earlier? That's a whole new thing."

"It's my conclusion," Claire said. "Conclusions are where the good stuff goes."

They were still arguing when Ms. Li called the class to order, and Claire read her essay aloud, feeling confident all the way to the final line. Ms. Li made one small red circle, around the last sentence only, and said nothing. Claire stared at that circle for the rest of class, because everything before it had passed without a single mark.

At recess she laid the pages out on the bench and read the conclusion over and over, hunting for the hidden problem. Then she noticed something. Her second paragraph was about safety, her third about wasted money, her fourth about healthier options, and her last paragraph did none of those jobs. Instead it said the same things again in fresh words, until the dance line arrived out of nowhere. She tried moving the dance argument up to become a fourth point, and suddenly the ending wrote itself, restating her position and gathering up her three reasons in new language.

"Your dance idea," she told Arie, running down the hall to find Ms. Li, "it gets its own paragraph now."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Japan's Obon festival, held in mid-August in most regions and in July in some, honors the spirits of ancestors, who are believed to return home for a visit.
story:
Piper had been in Japan for two weeks, staying with her aunt and a house full of cousins she barely knew, and everyone kept being kind to her in a way that made her throat hurt. It was their first summer without Gran, who had died in the spring, and Piper carried a flat envelope in her backpack that she could not bring herself to open. She presumed Gran had written it before the end, because the address on the front was in Gran's looping hand, and the word "Piper" was underlined twice.

At the gathering, cousins carried paper lanterns down to the river, and Piper followed without asking, because following was easier than talking. Her cousin Carl, who spoke English in bursts, kept glancing at her, and finally he said, "It's Obon. The lanterns are for the spirits."

"Spirits of who?" Piper asked.

"Ancestors. They come home for a visit," Carl said, and shrugged, as if this were the most obvious thing in the world. "Mid-August, Obon. Some places do it in July, but here it's August."

Piper turned that over all evening. If Gran's spirit was coming home for a visit, then home was across the ocean, and one paper lantern floating down a Japanese river could not possibly point that far. But then she thought about Gran, who used to say that letters were better than phone calls because a letter travels on its own, without wires, finding its person no matter what. Maybe a lantern worked the same way. She decided to test it. She wrote one line on her lantern with a marker: "Follow me home. Room at the top of the stairs." Then she lit it and set it on the dark water, watching it drift diagonal to the current, as if it had its own idea about where it was going.

That night, in her aunt's quiet house, Piper finally opened the envelope. Inside was a short letter in Gran's hand, dated months before. "When you miss me," it said, "do something with your hands. Bake, draw, build, write. Missing settles better when it has somewhere to go." Piper read it twice, then found paper and a pen and began to write back, one page, then another, while outside the river carried its small lights down toward the sea.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: An anecdote is a story about one person's experience; it cannot show that one thing caused another, because other explanations for what happened have not been ruled out.
story:
Natalie stood in aisle three of Miller's Pharmacy, staring at a shelf of magnetic bracelets, while her little brother banged a toy truck against her leg. The box said "Relieves pain naturally!" and next to it a card told about a man whose knee stopped hurting after two weeks of wearing one. Her grandmother wanted a birthday present for Uncle Ray, whose back had ached since spring, and Natalie had twenty dollars.

"That card's just one guy," said Savannah, appearing beside her with a basket of bandages. "Vincent's uncle has one of these and his back still hurts."

"But the card says it worked," Natalie said. She read it again. A man named Harold wore the bracelet, and his pain went away. She turned the box over, looking for a study, a trial, anything with tested results. There was nothing, just more stories.

"My cousin calls those anecdotes," Savannah said. "A story about one person's experience."

Natalie chewed her lip. "Okay, but Harold's back did get better. Something made it better."

"Maybe. But you can't know it was the bracelet." Savannah counted on her fingers. "Maybe his back was already getting better anyway. Maybe he started sleeping differently. Maybe he just felt like it worked."

"Because nothing else got ruled out," Natalie said slowly. It was like Vincent's model engine: you couldn't see inside the cylinder, but you could tell whether the piston was moving by watching the wheels. If the wheels turned without the piston, you'd know the piston wasn't the cause. Here, Harold got better, but there was no way to tell if the bracelet was what did it. "So one story can't show the bracelet fixed him. You'd have to test it on lots of people, with some wearing fake ones, so you could compare."

"Sounds complicated," Savannah said.

"A little." Natalie picked up the box anyway and carried it to the register, where Ms. Baptiste from down the street was buying cough syrup.

"That thing helped my shoulder, you know," Ms. Baptiste said, tapping the box. "Wore it a month, pain gone."

"Or it would've gone anyway," Natalie said. "Or you rested it more that month. Pain's kind of subjective too, right? Some days it feels worse and you can't say why."

Ms. Baptiste laughed. "Fair enough, smart girl. But it's a nice-looking bracelet."

That was true, Natalie thought. She paid for it, because Uncle Ray's birthday was Saturday and twenty dollars didn't stretch to a lab. But she slid a card into the gift bag, the one she'd written herself: "This might help your back. We don't actually know yet."

"Ready?" Savannah asked at the door.

"Ready," Natalie said, and pushed the door open into the bright afternoon.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: A dairy cow only produces milk after she has given birth to a calf.
story:
The permission slip had said fire station, so Anthony had spent the whole bus ride imagining ladders, hoses, and maybe a dalmatian. What he had not imagined was a poster of cows taped beside the front desk, right next to a stack of milk cartons for the firefighters' breakfast.

"They do a pancake fundraiser every month," Mr. Grewal explained as he led the class inside. "My brother's dairy farm donates the milk." He pointed at the poster. "That's his barn. Now, before anyone touches anything, the rules restrict you to the yellow line on the floor. Gear is heavy, and we move fast when the bell goes."

Alessandro raised his hand before Mr. Grewal had even finished. "Can we spray the hose? Please. I've been practicing holding the garden hose at home so I'd be ready."

"We'll see," said Mr. Grewal, which Anthony knew meant no, and Alessandro's shoulders sagged like a punctured air mattress.

While the others climbed into the truck cab, Anthony stayed by the poster. It showed two rows of cows in the milking barn, and behind the barn, in a smaller pen, a row of calves. He counted them. Twelve cows, and he counted twelve calves. He frowned and counted again, tapping the glass frame with one finger. That could not be a coincidence. Twelve and twelve.

He thought about his aunt's dog, who had never had puppies and never made milk, while Alessandro's cat had nursed kittens all spring. So the milk in the cartons by the desk came only from cows that had each had a calf. Every single one of them. He turned around, looking for someone to tell.

Stephen was standing at the worm bin in the station's little vegetable garden, where the firefighters composted lunch scraps. "Cool," Stephen was saying to Alessandro. "Worms are decomposers. They turn the old sandwiches into dirt." Anthony dragged them both to the poster.

"Count the cows," Anthony said. "Now count the calves."

Alessandro counted, then counted the calves a second time, his lips moving. "They match. Wait, so all of them? Every cow in that barn has had a calf?"

"That's why there's milk," Anthony said. "Only the ones who've had calves."

"Mr. Grewal!" Alessandro shouted across the bay, hand already up. "Is it true that every cow on your brother's farm has had a calf? Because if it is, can I please, please have the hose now?"

Mr. Grewal laughed, walked over, and unspooled a length of yellow practice hose. "One question at a time. And yes, every one of them." He pressed the lever, and water arced across the concrete, Alessandro gripping the nozzle with both hands.

activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
knowledge_domain: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
fact: Cash advances from a credit card usually carry a higher interest rate than purchases, plus a fee, and interest often starts right away.
story:
Simon had thirty-one dollars in the shoebox under his bed, and the telescope at Hartley's Hardware was on sale for fifty-five dollars until Sunday, when the sale ended and the price went back up. He figured his lemonade stand at the Saturday farmers' market could earn the rest, but only if he sold a lot. His friend Roy had already offered to close the gap. "Lend you twenty bucks," Roy had said, "and you pay me back twenty-five next week." Simon had said maybe, because something about it bothered him and he couldn't yet say what.

He set up his stand early, between Ms. Ricci's jam table and a man selling peppers. The morning was hot and the customers came in slow waves, so Simon kept a tally in his notebook, a little database of cups sold, quarters taken, and hours worked. Around ten, wasps invaded his pitcher, and he had to dump half of it and start over, which cost him time he could not get back.

While he was refilling, Ms. Ricci came back from the farm supply stall carrying an empty crate. She pulled a credit card from her wallet, slid it into the machine at the stall, and asked for forty dollars in cash. Before the cashier could press the button, Roy, who was stacking cups at Simon's stand, called over, "Ms. Ricci, wait. That's a cash advance. Cash advances on a credit card usually carry a higher interest rate than purchases, plus a fee, and the interest often starts right away." Ms. Ricci thanked him, put the card away, and wrote a check instead.

Simon stared at the machine as if it were a trap hidden under a friendly lid. The cash looked the same as any other cash, but it cost more just because of how you got it, and the clock on it started the second it touched your hand. He thought about last summer, when he had borrowed five dollars from Roy to buy a model rocket and had ended up mowing Roy's lawn twice to pay it back. He had told himself that was fine, but really it had taken him three weekends, and the rocket had sat in the garage half that time.

Now he did the math out loud, because that was how he kept himself honest. "Twenty now means twenty-five later," he told Roy. "That's five dollars for waiting one week. My stand earned eight dollars last Saturday. So one week of extra cost eats more than half a Saturday." Roy shrugged. "That's the deal, but you don't have to take it."

Simon turned back to his pitcher and made a fresh sign, bigger letters, colder cup, fifty cents. By two o'clock his database showed forty-two cups and nineteen dollars. By closing, the shoebox money and the day's takings added up to fifty-six dollars, and the sky was going purple over the pepper stall. Simon counted it twice, folded the bills into his pocket, and ran for Hartley's before the shutters came down.

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Double-acting baking powder releases gas twice: once when it gets wet in the batter and again when it is heated in the oven.
story:
Paisley tied her apron so tight the strings cut into her waist, because today she was getting the muffin station all to herself. Mr. Quinn had said the words she'd been waiting two months to hear: "Blueberry batch, start to finish, you." She flipped the recipe card over and read it again, hunting for anything that could trip her up. Preheat the oven to three seventy-five. She turned the dial and heard the elements tick and groan, and that sound felt like the starting gun of a race.

Then the race hit a wall. The oven was still holding a tray of Mr. Quinn's dinner rolls, and dinner rolls, apparently, could not be rushed. Behind her, Kaydence and Rowen were stacking dishes for the evening crowd, and Rowen called over, "Just let it sit, it's fine." Paisley stared at her bowl of batter, already mixed and wet, and felt her stomach drop. Wasn't batter like soda that had gone flat? Every minute on the counter had to be a minute of escaping bubbles, and the bubbles were the whole point of a muffin.

She said so, and Kaydence wandered over, drying her hands. "Read the can," Kaydence said, tapping the tin of baking powder on the shelf. Paisley picked it up and squinted at the small print. "Double-acting," she read out loud. The label said it released gas twice: once when it got wet in the batter, and again when it was heated in the oven. Paisley read it twice more, then looked at her batter with new eyes. The first wave of bubbles had already happened, right there in the bowl, which was the fizzing she'd noticed while stirring. But there was a second wave still waiting, and the second wave needed exactly the thing she was being forced to wait for: a hot oven.

Still, she wanted proof, not a label. So she made a plan worthy of a jury, even if Rowen groaned that it was trivial and she should just bake. "One bowl waits fifteen minutes, one bowl goes in the second the rolls come out," she said, and she kept them side by side so nobody could argue the comparison wasn't fair. When Mr. Quinn finally slid the rolls free, she filled two trays, muffin cups marching in rows, and slid them into the heat.

Twelve minutes later she crouched at the oven door, and there they were, the delayed ones, rising just as proudly as the fresh ones, crowns cracking golden above the rims. Both batches stood tall. The waiting hadn't ruined anything, and the second surge had carried them up exactly as promised. She pulled the trays out, set them on the rack, and carried the best-looking muffin across the kitchen with two hands, like something precious.

"Taste it," she said to Mr. Quinn, and held her breath while he broke it open and steam curled up into the light.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: As a broken bone heals, the body forms a callus, a mass of cartilage and new bone that bridges the gap between the broken ends.
story:
Alyssa sat on the bench by the hopscotch squares, her right arm stiff inside its purple cast, and watched Everley practice cartwheels for Friday's gymnastics assembly. Three days left, and Alyssa was supposed to be in the partner routine. Now all she could do was clap with one hand against her thigh, which felt like a privilege she no longer deserved.

"It won't humiliate you if you sit out," Everley said, landing a wobbly cartwheel. "Nobody expects a person with a broken arm to do a routine."

Alyssa wasn't listening, exactly. She was thinking about the fuzzy lump the doctor had shown her on the X-ray that morning. "That's your callus," the doctor had said, tapping the screen. "A mass of cartilage and new bone that bridges the gap between the broken ends." A bridge, she thought. Inside her arm, unseen, her body was building a little bridge of new bone across the break, stronger where it had snapped.

She turned the idea over. If the bone was already knitting together, maybe her arm wasn't as useless as it felt. Maybe it could hold weight now, gently, the way a new fence holds a vine if you don't yank it. There was one way to find out.

"Asiya," she called, "toss me the foam ball. Soft."

Asiya lobbed it in a slow arc. Alyssa lifted her casted arm, palm out, and the ball bounced off it with a hollow thump. A warm ache pulsed up to her elbow, but nothing shifted, nothing ground. She caught the next one. Then a third, harder, and her eyes watered, but the bridge held.

"So?" Everley came over, breathless.

"I can be your base," Alyssa said. "One arm steady, one arm out for balance. I felt it hold." She was surprised how optimistic she sounded, like someone had switched a light on inside her chest.

"Friday, then," Everley said, and held out her hand for a double high five.

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: Egyptian pyramids were built on the west bank of the Nile, the side where the sun sets, which Egyptians linked with death and the afterlife.
story:
Felix spread the giant map of Egypt across the library table and weighted the corners with three dictionaries and a stapler. His presentation was due tomorrow, and all he had was a title, "The Nile and the Pyramids," and a poster board so blank it seemed to be staring at him.

"Here's my problem," he told Lydia, who slid into the chair across from him. "I know the pyramids are huge. Everyone knows that. I know farmers depended on the Nile. But Mr. Moose said our grade comes from explaining why, not just listing what."

"So explain why," said Lydia.

"That's the problem." Felix tapped the map. "Nobody left us a manual."

Lydia leaned over the map with the meticulous care of someone who did not want to wrinkle it, and traced the blue squiggle of the river with one finger. "Wait. Look at this. The Nile runs through the whole map, and every pyramid marker is on the same side of it. Every single one."

Felix pulled the map closer and checked. She was right. The dots sat west of the river, all of them, like they were lining up for something. He felt the little spark he got when a pattern appeared out of nowhere.

"Not a coincidence," he said slowly. "When everything matches like that, something is causing it. But what?"

"Try the sunset," Lydia said. She pulled a scrap of paper, drew a river, and shaded one side. "The sun goes down over there. West. That's the side where the sun sets."

Felix stared at the paper. "The side where the sun sets," he repeated. Something shifted in his head, the way a locked door shifts before it opens. He flipped through the book he'd already read twice, hunting for the word he'd skipped past because it hadn't mattered yet. There. "Afterlife," he read aloud. "Egyptians linked the west side of the Nile with death and the afterlife. The sun sets in the west, and they connected that with..."

"With dying and coming back," Lydia finished. "Like the sun does. Every day."

"That's why they built them there." Felix grabbed a marker and started writing on his poster, then stopped. "Hold on. I need to clarify one thing before I put this in ink. This isn't just my guess, right? Let's check the second book." They checked. Then a third book, because Felix wanted to be sure. The fact held in all of them: west bank, sunset side, death and afterlife.

Ainsley wandered over from the computers, saw the poster, and frowned. "You know what's funny? My uncle restored an old farmhouse once and put the door on the sunrise side, and the neighbors were furious about it. People take directions seriously."

"That's kind of the whole point of my poster," Felix said, and realized it was true. "The river gave them food, the flood made the soil rich, and even where they buried their dead came from the sky."

At home that night, Felix finished the poster and set his alarm early. His backpack zipper caught on the way open, and his dad said the repair warranty had expired months ago, so Felix safety-pinned it shut and carried the poster flat in his arms, the Nile snaking down the middle, pyramids standing on the sunset side. In the morning, when Mr. Moose asked who wanted to present first, Felix raised his hand.

"Me," he said. "I've got a map and a question, and I want to show you something weird I found."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In East Asian dining etiquette, chopsticks should not be left standing upright in a bowl of rice, because it resembles incense offered to the dead.
story:
The potluck was in the gym after school, and Penelope had spent the whole bus ride rehearsing one goal: get Mr. Zhang to taste her grandmother's honey cake so he might sponsor the cooking club. She carried the plate on both palms like an offering, though she tried to conceal how nervous that made her, because Clara was walking beside her and Clara had her own plan.

"I'm going to hide my spring rolls behind the juice boxes," Clara said, lifting the lid to show the burnt, curled edges. "Nobody has to know I made them."

Tables ran along the walls, crowded with dishes from every household. Mr. Zhang had brought a slow-cooked beef stew, and the smell of it reached the door before they did. Van was already there, setting out bowls and chopsticks beside his mother's trays of dumplings, and he kept glancing at the gym entrance the way people do when they are waiting for someone in particular.

Penelope got her slice of cake onto Mr. Zhang's plate at last, and he smiled and said it looked wonderful, so she floated over to the rice table feeling almost buoyant. To free both hands for her water cup, she pushed her chopsticks straight down into her bowl of rice and let them stand there like two small flags. Across the table, Van's mother went very still, and Van set down his serving spoon and leaned toward Penelope, speaking quietly so only she could hear.

"Don't stand them up in the rice," he said. "That's how incense is offered to the dead."

Penelope pulled the chopsticks out so fast that grains of rice scattered across the tablecloth. She laid them sideways across the rim of her bowl instead, and Van nodded once, and his shoulders dropped, and she noticed that his mother was watching them both with a small breath of relief, the way you relax when something fragile has not broken after all.

Clara appeared at Penelope's elbow with an empty platter and a smug expression. "Somebody ate every single spring roll," she said. "Even the black ones. And guess what, Mr. Zhang asked me for the recipe." She pointed across the gym, where Mr. Zhang was on his second helping of stew, his chopsticks resting neatly on the little ceramic rest beside his bowl. Penelope looked at them, then at her own lying flat, and thought about all the rules that exist where you cannot see them, waiting quietly in a bowl of rice. Van's mother ladled more dumplings onto Penelope's plate and said, "Eat, eat, plenty more."

activity: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor
knowledge_domain: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor
fact: A cut that is still bleeding after 10 minutes of firm pressure needs medical help, and the pressure should continue until help arrives.
story:
Marcus had never been inside a driving school before, and he hadn't expected the Saturday first-aid class to smell like burnt coffee and old carpet, but there they were, twelve kids sitting in folding chairs behind a counter full of traffic cones. Mr. Guo, who taught driver's ed on weekdays, ran the class on weekends. He held up a roll of gauze and said, "Today you learn to patch a cut, and more importantly, when not to."

Marcus had signed up because his little cousin had split her chin at the pool last summer, and Marcus had just stood there, useless, while an adult did everything. He didn't want to feel that way twice.

"First practice," Mr. Guo said, "you keep pressure on the wound while I time you. Ten minutes is longer than you think." He paired Marcus with Noah, a tall kid from his school, and gave Marcus a marker line on his forearm to pretend was a cut. Marcus pressed a gauze pad over it. Noah clicked a stopwatch. After two minutes Marcus's arm ached. "Ten whole minutes?" he groaned, and Noah grinned and kept the timer running.

While they pressed, Mr. Guo told a short story about a driver who had fainted at the wheel, and how abrupt stops cause more injuries than slow ones. Then he read a line from his memoir-in-progress about thirty years of teaching nervous teenagers. Marcus half listened, because he was thinking about the timer. A minute took forever. If someone were actually bleeding, he realized, he'd want to check the cut way before ten minutes, to see if it was working. He raised his hand.

"Can I peek under the gauze to check?"

"You can," Mr. Guo said, "but you have to prioritize the rule over your curiosity. If you lift the pad early, you undo the work."

The stopwatch finally beeped at ten minutes. Marcus flexed his sore fingers and wrote the number on his worksheet: still bleeding after ten minutes of firm pressure means get a doctor, and keep pressing until help arrives.

He needed that fact three weeks later. Tye, who was in his grade, slipped on the ice outside the recreation centre and gashed his palm on a broken bottle. Blood welled up fast. Marcus grabbed his scarf, folded it into a pad, and pressed it hard against Tye's palm while a parent nearby called an ambulance. "You're okay," Marcus said. "I'm not letting go." He counted minutes in his head, out loud when he lost track. At ten minutes, the pad was still soaked through.

"Still bleeding," Marcus told the paramedic when she arrived, kneeling beside them with her bag open.

"Good work," she said, reaching for her shears. "Hold it right there while I get this wrapped."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, and the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10.
story:
The restaurant was loud before the game even started. Alexander slid into the booth between his friend Ariya and his grandpa, facing the big screen that stretched across the wall above the counter. His dad had promised wings, Isla was already arguing with Ariya about which team had the better quarterback, and somewhere behind them a server balanced six sodas on one tray.

"I remember the very first one of these," Grandpa announced, leaning back with his hands behind his head. "Watched it like it was yesterday."

Alexander looked up from his menu. Was that even possible? He tried to picture his grandpa young, sitting in some old living room, but the picture wouldn't come together. Instead of just wondering about it, he decided to test it, the way Ms. Mercado had shown them when they checked a claim in class: ask questions, then check the answers.

"Okay," Alexander said. "Who played?"

"The Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs." Grandpa said it without blinking. "Thirty-five to ten."

Ariya pulled out her phone before Alexander could ask anything else. "I'll look it up," she said, and then she frowned at the screen. "It's actually here. The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, and the Packers won 35 to 10 over the Chiefs."

"So what's the test?" Isla asked, dunking a fry in ketchup. "He got it right."

"He got it right twice," Alexander said slowly, watching his grandpa's face. "The teams and the score." There was still one thing bothering him, though, something he couldn't see directly. If Grandpa really remembered it, he wouldn't just know the facts anyone could look up. He'd remember the small stuff, the stuff that never made it onto a results page. "Grandpa, where were you sitting?"

Grandpa laughed. "On the floor, three feet from a television the size of a microwave, with my brother hogging the good pillow." He pointed a wing at Alexander. "That cushion had a hole in it, and the stuffing came out every time he sat down. I had the flat spot by the radiator."

"That's the test," Alexander said, grinning. "The score is the tedious part. Anyone can summarize that in one line. The pillow is the memory."

"It was an obligation to fight him for that pillow," Grandpa said solemnly. "Brothers' law."

The screen flashed and the crowd in the restaurant roared as the teams lined up for the opening kickoff. Ariya put her phone away, Isla raised her soda like a toast, and Grandpa wrapped one arm around Alexander's shoulders.

"Tell you what," Grandpa said. "You ask the questions, I'll remember the pillows. Deal?"

"Deal," said Alexander, and turned to face the big screen.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In France, friends often greet each other with cheek kisses called 'la bise', and the number of kisses varies from region to region.
story:
The restaurant smelled like butter and onions, and Liam's stomach growled even though he had promised himself he would not be hungry until everyone arrived. His family had a reservation for six o'clock sharp, because his cousins were catching a train back to Avignon at nine. That gave them three hours, his father kept saying, checking his watch like the train might leave early.

When the cousins walked in, Liam's cousin Théo grabbed his shoulders and kissed his right cheek, then his left. Two kisses. Then Théo's stepmother, Aunt Solène, leaned in and kissed his cheeks three times, first one side, then the other, then the first side again. Liam stood very still, the way you do when a bee lands near you, and tried to keep his face from showing how strange it felt.

"That's la bise," said Marguerite, who had come along because her mother knew Aunt Solène from university. "My grandmother does it too."

"But Théo did two," Liam whispered as they followed the waiter to a long table, "and she did three. Who's right?"

Marguerite shrugged. "They're French. They both are."

That answer did not sit well with Liam. If two people from the same country greeted differently, there had to be a reason, even if he could not see it. He decided to run a test. The last cousin to arrive, a tall girl named Céline, had driven down from Lyon. If she kissed him a certain number of times, maybe the number would match one of the others, and he could figure out who came from where, or at least who matched whom.

Céline arrived at 6:15, out of breath, holding a wrapped package for Liam's mother. She kissed Liam's cheeks twice. Théo grinned and kissed her back, twice, quick as a card shuffle. Aunt Solène got three from Celine, though, one for one. Interesting, Liam thought. Céline matched Théo with him, but matched Aunt Solène differently. Or Aunt Solène gave three to everyone, and that was her own pattern. He would need more data.

At the table, the customs kept coming. Miko, who had tagged along with Marguerite, put his elbows on the table and reached for the bread before anyone else, and Aunt Solène raised one eyebrow so slightly that only Liam noticed. He nudged Miko under the table and shook his head a tiny bit. Miko pulled his elbows in fast.

"This soup is nutritious," Aunt Solène said, ladling more into Liam's bowl, "and in our house you keep your hands visible, on the table, not in your lap." She demonstrated, hands resting beside her plate. Liam copied her.

Miko bit into the bread and gave it a serious critique. "Too crusty on the outside, perfect on the inside. Eight out of ten."

"Only an eight?" said Théo, pretending to be insulted. "In Lyon, this bread would be a nine."

"So you are from Lyon," Liam said suddenly. Two kisses, like Céline, who drove from Lyon.

Théo blinked, then laughed. "And my stepmother is not. She kisses three times, like her whole family does where she grew up."

Liam wanted to ask where exactly, but the waiter appeared with the main course, and his father tapped his watch. Two hours to the train. Aunt Solène leaned over and kissed Liam's cheek three times, quick and warm.

"Eat," she said.

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: When two identical bulbs are wired in series to one battery, each glows more dimly than a single bulb would on the same battery.
story:
Hannah pressed the switch and the little bulb on her model lighthouse blinked on, a small orange dot in the middle of the museum's workshop table. Ms. Chen had set out batteries, switches, wires, and bulbs, and the task was posted on the wall: build a circuit and explain why the bulb lights.

"It works because it's a loop," Hannah said to Shyla, tracing the wire with one finger. "From the battery, through the switch, through the bulb, and back. Break the loop anywhere and it stops." She flipped the switch off and on twice to prove it, and the bulb obeyed her each time.

That was when Hallie leaned over from the next table. "Your lighthouse only has one light. Real lighthouses have two." She held out a second, identical bulb. "Here. Brighter is better, right?"

Hannah wondered about that. Would a second bulb add light, or would something be shared between them? She couldn't see what traveled in the wire, only what happened at the ends, so she decided to test it. She unclipped one wire, clipped in the second bulb so the current had to pass through one and then the other, and pressed the switch.

Both bulbs lit. But each one glowed more dimly than her single bulb had on the same battery, two pale coins instead of one bright one. "Huh," Shyla said, watching. "It's dimmer, not brighter."

"It's called series," Hallie said, reading the label on the parts bin. "When they're wired like that."

Hannah tried moving a wire so the second bulb sat on its own branch instead. Pressing the switch again, she watched both bulbs, and her mood went buoyant, like the foam boats floating in the wave tank across the room. "Look at that," she said. "Try it with three."

Ms. Chen stopped behind them, but she only smiled and let them clip.

activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel
knowledge_domain: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel
fact: In Lord of the Flies, the beast the boys fear on the mountain turns out to be the body of a dead airman under a parachute, which they mistake for a monster.
story:
Aiden had until Monday, and Ms. Do had been clear: the reading log needed one symbol traced across at least three chapters, with evidence. He wedged himself into the reading nook by the window with Lord of the Flies, a pad of sticky notes, and a bag of pretzels he was supposed to save for later.

The beast was the obvious choice. In the early chapters the littleuns just talked about it, a snake-thing in the dark. He marked that page. Later, the twins claimed something with claws and teeth, and he marked that too. On his notepad he wrote "the beast gets more real every time they talk about it," which felt almost clever until he stared at it and thought, so what? He needed the moment where it changed into something bigger, and Ms. Do wanted him to say why.

His mom knocked and set a mug of cocoa on the shelf beside him without a word, because she knew he forgot to eat when he was buried in a book. He mouthed thank you and kept flipping.

Then he found the mountain scene again, and it stopped him cold. The shape the boys saw hunched on the mountaintop, the thing they fled from in terror, was not a monster at all. Rereading with that knowledge, Aiden saw the whole scene differently: the twisted figure in the dark was the body of a dead airman tangled in his parachute. The boys had mistaken it for the beast. He sat back so fast he knocked the pretzels onto the cushions.

That was it. The beast was not a thing; it was fear wearing whatever shape the dark offered. He grabbed the phone and called Audrey, who had chosen the conch for her log.

"Wait, the beast on the mountain isn't real?" she said.

"It's a dead pilot under a parachute," Aiden said. "They looked at it and saw a monster."

"So your symbol colonizes the whole book," Audrey said. "First the beast is just talk, then it takes over everything they do."

"I don't want the fear to have a monopoly on my essay, though," Aiden said. "The conch and the fire have to count too."

"Then be impartial," Audrey said. "Give each one its paragraph."

He laughed, picked the pretzels off the cushions one by one, and started writing in the margin of his notepad: Chapter six, reread, shape on the mountain.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A claim that cannot be checked even in principle, such as a vague promise that something 'changes lives,' gives readers nothing to test.
story:
The advertisement was taped to the back of the seat in front of Taylor, and she had read it eleven times by the time the bus reached the bridge. BUILD YOUR BRAIN POWER, it said in enormous letters. THE MINDCAP SYSTEM CHANGES LIVES. Below that, a boy about her age grinned beside a trophy. "He looks happy," Taylor said to Ayoub, who was squished in beside her with his backpack on his lap. "But how would you ever know if it changed lives? Changed them how? Compared to what?"

Ayoub leaned around the seat to look. "Maybe it means your grades go up." Taylor thought about that. A grade going up was a thing you could check. You could look at report cards from before and after. You could count. But "changes lives" wasn't like that. "A claim you can't check even in principle gives you nothing to test," she said slowly, trying the idea out loud. "Like if I told you my lucky sock makes the weather better. You couldn't ever prove me wrong, because I could say any rainy day was going to be worse without the sock." Ayoub laughed so hard the driver glanced in the mirror.

"Then test it," Ayoub said. So Taylor did. She turned to Lennox across the aisle. "Lennox, I have a pencil that changes lives." Lennox narrowed her eyes. "Changes them how?" "Just changes them," Taylor said. "Buy it for a dollar." Lennox folded her arms. "Then if nothing happens you'll say something did happen, and I can't catch you lying. No deal." Behind Lennox, Ms. Watanabe, who rode the afternoon route to the community center, was smiling without looking up from her book.

Taylor pulled out her notebook and made two columns. On the left she wrote things you could check: precipitation totals for Tuesday, whether the vending machine had run out of granola bars, whether Ayoub's little sister had actually cleaned the desolate corner of their garage like she'd promised. On the right she wrote the MindCap ad. That column stayed strange and empty, like a promise floating loose from any proof. "I'm going to write to the company," she announced. "I'll ask them to justify the trophy. If the boy really won it, they can name the contest."

"Contest nobody's ever heard of," Lennox said, holding out her hand anyway. "And I still want to see the pencil."

"I knew you'd ask," Taylor said, and dug through her backpack for it.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Avoiding everything that causes anxiety brings quick relief but often makes the anxiety stronger over time, because the person never learns the situation is manageable.
story:
Clara sat cross-legged on her bed with her science notes in her lap and her door firmly closed. In two weeks she had to present her project on tide pools in front of the whole class, and her stomach had already started its familiar tightening. Last month she had pretended to be sick to skip the history presentation. The month before that, she had asked Ms. Ho if she could hand in a written report instead. Each time she got out of it, the wave of relief was enormous, like sinking into a hot bath. But something strange had been nagging at her, and tonight she turned it over in her mind. Was it her imagination, or did each presentation feel scarier than the last?

She picked up her phone and called Calla. "Can I ask you something weird? When you skip something that makes you anxious, does it get easier or harder the next time?"

"Harder, obviously," Calla said. "I skipped the spring concert in grade five because of the stress, and the fall concert felt ten times worse. Why?"

Clara chewed her pencil eraser, skeptical of her own half-formed reasoning. "I keep thinking skipping is like resting, but what if it's more like watering a weed?" She stared at the tide pool poster leaning against her wall, its green paper smelling faintly of markers. Maybe avoiding things didn't shrink the fear. Maybe it fed it.

"Test it," Calla said. "Do a tiny version tonight."

So Clara set her twelve stuffed animals in a row on the rug, her oldest bear propped on the pillow like a strict judge. Her hands shook when she stood up and said, "Tide pools form where the ocean meets the rocks." Her voice cracked on "ocean." She did it again, and again, noticing that by the fifth round her breathing had slowed, the way her mom regulated the kitchen timer, little by little, until the noise faded. The room was warm and smelled like pencil shavings, and outside a dog barked twice and went quiet.

The next morning she told Ms. Ho, "I want to try presenting, but can I go first, before I talk myself out of it?" Ms. Ho raised an eyebrow and wrote her name at the top of the list. Walking back to her seat, Clara's heart still hammered, but it felt like a hammer building something instead of breaking it. Could the fear actually shrink if she stopped running? She was curious enough to find out. On presentation day she stood up, took one breath, and said, "Tide pools form where the ocean meets the rocks."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Muscle soreness after new or hard exercise usually peaks 24 to 72 hours later, not right away; this is called delayed onset muscle soreness.
story:
Kate had been fine after the first soccer practice of the season. She'd walked home easy, eaten dinner, and thought this team stuff would be simple. Then Thursday morning came, and she could barely get down the stairs. Her thighs burned with every step, and by the time she reached the field for the evening session, she was walking like a stiff-legged robot.

"You were flying around on Tuesday," said Coraline, jogging beside her across the frost-silvered grass, her breath hanging in the cold air like vapor. "Now you look like a grandma."

"That's the weird part," Kate said. "Tuesday I felt great. Better than great. And yesterday, only a little sore. Today is the worst." She frowned at her own legs as though they had betrayed her on purpose. Something didn't add up. If practice had hurt her, the hurt should have shown up right after practice. Instead it had crept up two days later, like a bill arriving late.

During the warm-up, she watched her teammates. Aviana, who was new to the team, sprinted hard and laughed the whole time, bouncing on her toes. But the girls who'd been at Tuesday's session were all moving carefully, wincing when they crouched. Kate counted them. Every single one. The ones who'd played hard on Tuesday were sore today, and the soreness hadn't peaked right after practice, it had peaked one, two, even three days later. That was a pattern. It meant the pain wasn't caused by anything happening today.

She tested her idea on her mother that night, wincing dramatically on the second stair. "It's a real thing," she reported. "It peaks twenty-four to seventy-two hours later, not right away. Aviana looked it up after I told her about it. It's called delayed onset muscle soreness." She said the words slowly, like they were a password.

At Saturday's game, Kate still ached a little, but she'd figured out the timing, so she'd taken it easier in the drills on Thursday, and the worst had passed. The team they faced was from the affluent side of town, with matching bags and a coach who tried to recruit half their players over the summer, or so Coraline claimed. Kate didn't care about any of that. In the second half, with the score tied, she saw Aviana open near the box, planted her sore but willing legs, and swung.

"Pass it, pass it!" screamed Aviana.

The ball left her foot and curved through the cold air toward the goal.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A primary source is a firsthand record from the time, such as a letter, photograph or official data, and it is often the best place to check a claim.
story:
Antoine was on the family computer in the kitchen, hunting through the town library's old newspaper archive, when his mom set a paper bag on the counter. "Your grandmother's prescription is in there," she said. "Don't knock it in the sink."

"I won't," Antoine said, though he barely looked up. He had a problem. His classmate Brycen had sworn up and down at lunch that the town was founded by a man named Cyrus Hale, who according to Brycen had single-handedly built the first house, the first mill, and the first school. Mr. Grewal had assigned a short report on the town's founding, and Antoine had a nagging feeling that Brycen's version was more story than fact. The trouble was, Brycen sounded so certain.

Antoine set the archive search to 1850 through 1870 so it would exclude everything after the town's early years. If Hale had really done all that, the papers from that time would say so. He scrolled through grainy scans, squinting at headlines about a flammable warehouse that had burned down twice before the town bought a proper fire pump. Then he found it: a letter to the editor, written in 1861 by a woman named Sarah Ellery, who described arriving with her family on the first wagon train. She wrote that the first house had been raised by eleven families working together, and that the mill was built by her own father and two neighbours. There was even a photograph printed beside the letter, a blurry picture of the mill with a dozen people standing in front of it.

Antoine sat back. The paper from 1861 was a firsthand record from the time. He'd heard Mr. Grewal say the words once, half-asleep in class: "a primary source." This was exactly that, a letter and a photograph straight from the people who were there. Brycen's version had come from a souvenir pamphlet printed for the town's hundredth birthday, which glorified one man and left everyone else out. Antoine checked two more letters and a land office report, and they all matched Ellery's account.

The next morning Antoine brought printouts to school and spread them on the desk beside Brycen's. "Look, this is a primary source," he said, tapping the letter. "It's from 1861, from someone who was actually here."

Brycen frowned at the photograph of the mill crew, then at his own pamphlet. "So Cyrus Hale didn't build all that alone?" He turned the pamphlet over, as if the truth might be hiding on the back. "Man. I told my whole family that story at dinner." He picked up the printout of Ellery's letter and read it slowly, all the way to the signature. "Okay. We're writing about the eleven families instead. Can I use your copy of the photo?"

Antoine slid it across the desk and grinned. "Make it big. She's the one standing at the front with the hammer."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: One of the first written guides to online manners, 'Netiquette Guidelines', was published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855.
story:
"Nobody types in all caps. That's rule one," Alexia said, holding her phone so Nicholas could see the new group chat she was making for their science class.

Nicholas leaned closer. "But what about rule two? And who decides these rules anyway? Did someone just make them up on the spot, or is there an actual official list somewhere?" He wondered about that. It felt strange that everyone seemed to know you shouldn't spam a chat with forty crying-laughing emojis, yet nobody had ever taught him that in school.

Donovan, sprawled on the rug with his own phone, nominated himself as the person who would look it up, because according to him he was "basically a professional researcher." He typed fast, then went quiet, which built real suspense, because Donovan going quiet was like a parrot going quiet. "Okay, this is weird," he finally said. "There's a real document. It's from 1995 and it's called RFC 1855."

"It's called the Netiquette Guidelines," Nicholas read over his shoulder. "Netiquette. Like etiquette, but for the net." He scanned the old document, amazed that people in 1995 were already worried about typing in all caps, which apparently meant shouting back then too. Some things, it seemed, never changed. He decided to test an idea. "Alexia, send a message to your mom in all caps and see what she does."

Alexia texted her mother, who was downstairs: "CAN I HAVE A SNACK." The reply came in ten seconds: "Why are you yelling at me?"

The three of them cracked up, and even the cat jumped at the noise. Nicholas realized something else while laughing: in a private text, all caps just looked silly, but in the big public group chat, caps would feel like an announcement to twenty-six people at once. Same words, different room, different weight. That was probably why the old guide bothered to separate the two. "So rule one stands," he said. "And rule two: no caps unless it's an emergency, a volcano, or Donovan's spontaneous dance videos."

"Those are definitely emergencies," Donovan said, already recording one.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A percentage based on very few attempts can be misleading: a player who makes one shot out of one attempt shoots 100 percent.
story:
Bentley flopped onto the couch with the newspaper sports section, which was unusual, because his social studies project was due tomorrow morning and the article he needed was supposed to be somewhere in the living room. His mother had promised to postpone the vacuuming until he found it, but she kept hovering with the vacuum like a shark.

"Have you seen the green folder?" he asked Haylee, who was sprawled on the rug doing the same project. "Mine has the stats page in it."

"Stats," Haylee said, without looking up. "You know who loves stats? Hope. She's been texting me all afternoon because some girl on her basketball team is bragging about a perfect shooting percentage."

"Perfect?" Bentley sat up. "Hope's team lost half its games."

"That's what I said." Haylee held up her phone so he could see the message. "Hope says this girl made one shot all season. One. She took one shot, it went in, and now she's telling everyone she shoots a hundred percent."

Bentley stared at the phone. Something about it snagged in his brain, the way a shoelace catches in a door. "One shot out of one attempt," he said slowly. "So her percentage is technically true, but it doesn't mean anything. If she'd taken twenty shots and missed nineteen, nobody would brag."

"So Hope should call her out?" Haylee asked.

"Or make her take more shots." Bentley grabbed a pencil and wrote on the margin of the newspaper, because that was how he thought. "Watch. One for one is a hundred percent. But my brother's friend took fifty shots and made thirty-one. That's worse as a percentage, but way more real."

Haylee squinted at the numbers. "The newspaper does this too. Look, this pitcher is ranked fourth, but the tiny print says he only pitched two games."

"Exactly." Bentley flipped the page, and there, wedged between a ranking of city teams and a durable old coffee stain, was his stats page, printed right in the sports section. "Ha! Found it. I can finish the project and vacuum is cancelled."

His mother appeared in the doorway, vacuum humming hopefully.

"Postponed," Bentley announced, holding up the page like a trophy. "Permanently."

Haylee laughed so hard she knocked over the pencil cup, and as the pencils rolled across the rug, she said, "You should tutor Hope's teammate in math."

"Better idea," Bentley said, and started typing a message to Hope: "Challenge her to take ten shots tomorrow. Then we'll see the real percentage."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Joining a club or team at a new school puts a student in regular contact with the same people who share an interest, which gives friendships time to grow.
story:
The first day at her new school, Lea ate lunch alone at the end of a long table, and by Friday she was still eating alone. She watched the other kids, and she noticed something. The ones who seemed to have friends weren't the loudest ones or the friendliest ones. They were the ones who kept showing up in the same small groups, day after day, doing the same thing together. Her old friends back home hadn't appeared out of nowhere either. Baylee had sat beside her in art class all through fourth grade, and Alena had been on her soccer team for two seasons. Friendship, Lea decided, was not something you could ask for. It was something that grew when the same people kept meeting around something they all liked.

That was the hidden rule, and she thought she could test it. On Monday she found the club list taped outside the office. Chess club met every Tuesday and Thursday in Mr. Fernando's room, and you didn't have to be good. She had played with her grandfather, nothing more, but that hardly mattered. What mattered was that the same people would be there twice a week, every week, and they would all share one interest. If her idea about friendship was right, that room was where it would happen.

Her first Tuesday was rough. Two boys named nothing to her were halfway through a game and barely looked up. She sat down across from a girl and lost in eleven moves. "You moved your queen out too early," the girl said, not unkindly. Lea realized she had been biased against the whole club before she even walked in, assuming a room of strangers would stay strangers. That was exactly the kind of thinking she was supposed to be testing.

That night she wrote to Baylee, because Baylee would understand a plan better than anyone.

Dear Baylee, Chess club experiment, day one. Hypothesis: if I participate every single meeting, the same people and I will have time to become friends, because we all like the same thing. Results so far: lost badly, learned the queen thing, girl's name is Alena (different Alena than ours). Will report back. Missing you. Lea.

By the third week she had a standing game with the new Alena every Thursday. By the fifth week, when Lea executed a pivot nobody expected, trading her rook to trap Alena's king in the corner, half the room leaned over their boards to watch, and Alena laughed and demanded a rematch. Mr. Fernando started saving the seat by the window for them.

In November, Alena slid her sandwich across the lunch table and said, "You're sitting with us today, no arguments." Lea sat.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: A canoe is most stable when paddlers keep their weight low and centered, which is why people step into the middle of a canoe rather than onto its side.
story:
Stella had been at camp for exactly one day, and she already resented the canoe. It sat at the dock like it was waiting to trick her, rocking on the green lake water whenever anyone came near. Her cabin-mate Lukas stood beside her in an orange life jacket, gripping a paddle with both hands.

"Race starts in twenty minutes," said Mae, jogging up from the lodge. "Mr. Delgado says we need two per boat. Stella, you're with Lukas."

Lukas swallowed. "I flipped a canoe once. At my cousin's lake. I stepped in and the whole thing went over like a teeter-totter."

Stella looked at the canoe, then at the water, then back at the canoe. Yesterday she had watched the older campers load their boats. They hadn't climbed in the way Lukas described. They had done something different, and she tried to picture it. They stepped right into the middle, keeping low, almost crouching, and they stayed low while they sat down too. She had also noticed that when one girl leaned way out over the side to grab a floating hat, the boat tipped hard. When they kept their weight centered, it barely moved at all.

"Watch this first," Stella said. She held the canoe steady against the dock, then stepped carefully onto the floor in the middle, knees bent, and knelt onto the seat. The canoe wobbled a little and then settled, flat and calm. "See? Middle, low down. Try it." Lukas put one foot on the gunwale, the rim at the side, and the canoe lurched so hard Stella grabbed the dock. "Not there! The edge is the wobbly part. Middle of the canoe. Stay low." He pulled his foot back, held his breath, and stepped down into the center. The boat hardly swayed.

"That's the strangest thing I've ever felt," Lukas said, grinning. "It's like the boat wants you there."

At the starting line, ten canoes bobbed in a row. The counselor raised a flag and shouted, and paddles hit the water all at once. Stella kept her strokes even and reminded Lukas to keep his weight centered when he reached across to paddle on her side. Around the second buoy they passed Mae's boat, whose two paddlers were leaning out at opposite angles, and Mae shouted, "Not fair! You two look like you're sitting on a couch!"

"That's because we're in the middle!" Lukas called back.

At the finish, the counselor announced the results with strict impartiality, reading times off her clipboard. Stella and Lukas came in third. As they hauled the canoe up onto the sand, dripping and laughing, Lukas turned over a wet log at the edge of the beach to look for a decomposer for his nature-club checklist, and a beetle the size of his thumbnail scurried for shade.

"There's one," Stella said, crouching beside him in the warm sand. "Want to flip the log back over so it can get home?"

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: In a 1950 study of a student housing complex at MIT, Leon Festinger and colleagues found residents most often became friends with the people who lived closest to them.
story:
The moving truck pulled away, and Noah stood on the sidewalk of a street where every house was unfamiliar. Back home he had Ray and Tiffany and a whole soccer team, but here he had eleven boxes still sealed in the garage and a street called Juniper Lane where nobody knew his name. His dad handed him a trash bag and said to pick up the packing debris while he signed some papers inside.

Noah was pulling a flattened box out of the hedge when a girl rode past on a bike, circled the cul-de-sac twice, and stopped at the house directly across the street. "You the new kid," she said. It wasn't really a question. "I'm Tiffany. That's my brother's old bike." She rode off before he could answer, but that night Noah lay awake thinking. His old best friend, Ray, had lived one house down from him since kindergarten. Tiffany lived across the street. Maybe there was a rule about this, some pattern about who becomes friends with whom, and he wanted to find it.

The next morning he searched the garage for something to read and found a box marked DAD, COLLEGE. Inside were old psychology textbooks, and one had a chapter with a citation that caught his eye: a 1950 study of a student housing complex at MIT, by Leon Festinger and colleagues. Noah read the sentence twice. The residents of that complex had most often become friends with the people who lived closest to them. Not the nicest people, not the people with the best bikes. The closest ones.

He decided to test it. If the pattern was real, he could presume that his nearest neighbors were his best shot, so he should stop waiting for somebody perfect to appear. His baseball glove had been dormant in a box since the move, still smelling like his old field, so he oiled it, carried it outside, and began tossing a ball against his own garage door. Whap. Whap. Whap.

Mr. Pelletier, the retired man next door, came out to get his mail and watched for a minute. "You play?" he asked.

"Pitcher," Noah said. "Well, mostly outfield, honestly."

"There's boys two doors down who play every afternoon," Mr. Pelletier said, pointing with his mail. "And the girl across the street has a mean arm. I've seen her."

Tiffany appeared on her porch as if she had been waiting for exactly this. "You throw against a garage door all day or do you actually want to play?" she called.

Noah tucked his glove under his arm and crossed the street.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: An opinion supported with evidence is still an opinion, but it is a more convincing one than an opinion given with no reasons.
story:
The group chat lit up at 7:42 on a Tuesday night, right after Jace had set his phone on the kitchen table to charge. Nineteen messages. He scrolled to the beginning and found the source: Mario had posted a photo of the empty lot behind the rec center with the words "They're building a parking garage here, my cousin works for the city." By the time Jace caught up, half the class was arguing about where the skateboard ramps would go, and Kyrie had already sent three messages nobody answered.

Jace typed, "Wait. Is this real?" Mario answered fast. "My cousin said so." A thumbs-up emoji appeared under it, then another. Jace stared at the photo. The lot was just cracked asphalt and weeds, same as it had been since March. Nothing in the picture conveyed anything about a garage; it was just a lot. Mario's cousin might be right, but Jace couldn't see the cousin, couldn't see a plan, couldn't see anything except weeds.

He texted Mario directly, outside the group chat. "Can you ask your cousin for the paperwork? Like a notice or something?" Then he walked to the lot himself, because it was two blocks away and his mom said fine as long as he was back by eight. Taped to the fence was a bright orange sheet. He read it twice under the streetlight: soil testing, and a public meeting at the library on Thursday about a community garden. He photographed it and sent it to the chat.

The messages that followed came slowly at first. Mario wrote, "Okay so not a garage." Then Kyrie, who never typed in all caps, typed in all caps: "THIS IS WHY I CHECK THINGS." She sent a photo of her own notebook, open to a page where she had counted cars and recorded eleven near-misses at the corner of Maple and Third, all in one week, all because kids crossed there to get to school with no crosswalk. Below her tally she had written a short letter to the city asking for a painted crossing and a sign. "It's my opinion that we need a crosswalk," she typed. "The eleven near-misses don't make it a fact, they just make my opinion way more convincing than 'somebody should do something.'"

Jace read that message three times. He thought about the garage. Mario had given a reason, his cousin, but not a checkable one, and it had still fallen apart. Kyrie had given reasons that could be counted on a street corner, and even though a crosswalk remained her opinion, the city would have a harder time ignoring eleven near-misses than zero reasons. He typed, "Opinion with evidence beats opinion with nothing," and Kyrie replied, "Exactly. Still an opinion though."

On Thursday, Jace and Mario went to the library meeting with Kyrie. The room smelled like old paper and someone's coffee, and a man from the city stood at the front holding a stack of comment cards. Kyrie raised her hand and read her tally out loud, all eleven, one by one, including the morning a delivery truck honked so long that a third grader dropped his backpack in the road. The man from the city wrote something down. "Eleven," he repeated, and underlined it twice.

Afterward, walking home, Mario kicked a pebble along the sidewalk and said, "Next time I'll check before I post." Jace pulled out his phone and opened a new message to Kyrie. "You free Saturday to count cars at Maple and Third? More numbers, better odds." She answered with one word: "Yes."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: Older adults are at greater risk of hypothermia, a dangerous drop in body temperature, than younger adults.
story:
Colton had until six o'clock, when the market closed, to find a blanket thick enough for Grandpa Ray, whose bus arrived at seven. Grandpa Ray was staying for a whole week, and he had already made one thing clear on the phone: "Don't fuss over me, kid. I've survived worse than a little cold snap." The house, though, had an old furnace and a drafty guest room, and Colton didn't like the math on that.

He found Josie at the secondhand stall, holding up a quilt with moose on it. "For your grandpa?" she asked. "Perfect. Moose are basically the biggest herbivore in North America, so it's like the blanket is on his side."

"It's not about looking tough," Colton said, but he took the quilt anyway. That was when he noticed something odd. Grandpa Ray had slept in the guest room last Christmas, and Colton remembered shivering under two blankets himself while Grandpa Ray claimed he was "fine, just fine." Colton had assumed the room was fine too. Now he wasn't so sure. Grandpa Ray never complained, so the complaining couldn't be the signal. There had to be another way to know if the cold was actually a problem.

At the pharmacy counter near the market's back wall, a small paper flyer sat in a rack, and Mr. Bear, who ran the hardware stall and made the long commute in from the county every Saturday, nodded at it while counting change. Colton read the flyer twice. Older adults, it said, are at greater risk of hypothermia, a dangerous drop in body temperature, than younger adults. He frowned. "Hypothermia," he said out loud, testing the word.

"Deadly serious stuff in a cold bedroom," Mr. Bear said, handing a customer his receipt. "Folks your grandpa's age can slip into it without ever feeling properly cold."

That was the missing piece, Colton realized. It wasn't that Grandpa Ray was braver than everyone else. His body just might not sound the alarm the way a twelve-year-old's would, so "I'm fine" couldn't be trusted as evidence. Colton bought the moose quilt, then jogged to the hardware stall and bought a small electric heater with the birthday money in his pocket. Ria, working her mom's produce stand, waved him through the crowd. "Five forty-five! You've got fifteen minutes!"

He made it to the register just as the lights over the doors dimmed. At seven, he was standing at the bus stop, quilt under one arm, heater under the other. When Grandpa Ray stepped down and saw him, he laughed. "Told you not to fuss."

"I'm not fussing," Colton said. "I'm running an experiment. The heater goes in your room, and the quilt goes on your bed, and you don't get a vote." He held out the quilt so the moose were facing up. "Also, Ria says moose are on your side."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer is called the equilibrium price, or market-clearing price.
story:
Sofia had exactly forty minutes before her mom picked her up, and the box she wanted was already drawing a crowd. It sat on a card table at Mr. Yang's garage sale, packed with old comic books, and a handwritten sign taped to the front said $2 each.

"They'll be gone in ten minutes," Maxx said, reading over her shoulder.

"Then we have ten minutes to be smart," Sofia said. She watched the table instead of the comics. Two boys from another school were flipping through the box fast, keeping every third issue. A woman in a sun hat took five. Mr. Yang, folding shirts nearby, noticed it too. He peeled the sign off the table and wrote a new one: $5 each. The buyers slowed down, but they kept coming, and by the time Santino jogged up the driveway, the box was nearly empty.

"Five dollars for these?" Santino said. "Last month at the school sale they were a dollar."

"There were stacks of them there," Sofia said. "Here there are eight left and everybody wants one." She counted the remaining comics twice, watching who picked one up and who put it back. At five dollars, four people walked away. Mr. Yang crossed out the five and wrote three. Two more comics went. Then he wrote two, and the last two issues sold before Santino finished arguing.

"Wait," Sofia said slowly, testing it out loud. "Five was too high because some were left over. Two was too low because they went too fast. Three was the price where the amount people wanted matched the amount he had." She grinned. "When the buyers who want it equal what the seller offers, that's the equilibrium price. Market-clearing."

"Clearing the market," Mr. Yang said, patting the empty box. "My niece taught me that word. Garage sales are fertile ground for it, believe me. Commerce at its humblest."

"Then it conquered me," Santino said, holding his wallet, "because I got nothing."

Sofia counted her money and looked down the street toward the yellow house with the second sign on its lawn. "Twenty-five minutes left. Run."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks do not count as at-bats, so the number gives a batter no credit for walks.
story:
Alexandre slid into a seat two rows behind the home bench, next to Andy, who was already scrolling through stats on his phone. The gym smelled like popcorn and floor wax, and the junior varsity game before theirs was still winding down. "Kapoor says we should scout the other team," Andy said, turning the screen around. "Their best guy averages eighteen points a game." Alexandre frowned at the number. Eighteen points sounded terrifying, but it was only one number for a whole season of games, and he wanted to know what was hiding underneath it.

Last summer, Alexandre had made an impulsive bet with his cousin about a baseball player, and it still stung. He had insisted the player was terrible because his batting average was low, and his cousin had laughed at him. "A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats," his cousin had said, "and walks don't count as at-bats." Then his cousin pointed at the player's walk total, which was enormous, and Alexandre realized the average had been quietly ignoring every single time the player got on base for free. The number wasn't lying exactly, but it was only telling part of the story, and Alexandre had lost five dollars finding that out.

Now he leaned over Andy's shoulder. "Eighteen a game. But how does he get it? Does he shoot a lot, or is he efficient?" Andy scrolled to the game log. Twenty-three points on Tuesday, but only six on Friday, and on Friday the box score showed nine assists. "Look at this," Alexandre said, tapping the screen. "Friday they doubled him every time, and he just passed. The average squishes all of that into one number." Andy grinned. "So if we shut him down like that other team did, the eighteen doesn't mean anything."

Mr. Kapoor, who coached their team, crouched beside their seats during the timeout. "You two look like you're doing homework instead of watching." Alexandre showed him the game log, the low Friday, the nine assists. Mr. Kapoor's eyebrows went up. "Well," he said, "you've done more scouting than I have. You're starting on defense tonight, Alexandre. Face-guard him and make him give it up."

When the game started, Alexandre stuck to the shooter like a shadow, arms up, refusing to bite on the first fake even though the crowd groaned for him to chase everything. Late in the second quarter the boy passed instead of shot, again and again, and his teammates weren't ready for it. After the buzzer, Andy found Alexandre by the water bottles and clapped him on the shoulder. "He finished with twelve. The average will say he had a bad week, and it'll be partly because of you." Alexandre grinned and pulled his shoes back on. "Then let's make it a bad month."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The crowd 'wave' became known worldwide at the 1986 FIFA World Cup in Mexico, so many English speakers outside North America call it the Mexican wave.
story:
Layla counted the people squeezed into Ms. MacLeod's living room and decided the big game was better with a crowd, even if the crowd included Nolan, who rooted for the other team on purpose. Ms. MacLeod had hauled out a second bowl of popcorn and told everyone to cheer as much as they liked, as long as nobody stood on the couch again.

In the second half, the camera showed the packed stadium doing the wave. Thousands of people leapt up section by section, a ribbon of motion rolling all the way around the bowl. Layla's cousin, who was staying with her family for the summer and talked like a character from a movie, jumped up and pointed at the screen. "There! That's the Mexican wave!"

"That's not what it's called," Layla said. "It's just the wave."

"It got famous at the 1986 World Cup in Mexico," her cousin said, "so everyone back home calls it the Mexican wave."

Layla figured he was teasing her, the way he teased her about how she said "tomato." She decided to test it instead of arguing. "Ms. MacLeod, what do you call that?"

"The Mexican wave, love. Why, what do you call it?"

Nolan shrugged. "The wave. But my grandma calls it that too, and she's from Trinidad."

"So it's a place thing, not a made-up thing," Layla said. "Huh. Jovan's cousin from Spain probably calls it something else entirely." She filed that away as a question for Monday.

While she was standing there feeling clever, she noticed her arms had goosebumps for the third time that afternoon. The room kept going cold in waves too, which was odd, because the house was warm as toast between chills. Someone was touching the thermostat, and nobody was admitting it. "Nolan," she said slowly, "are you implying you had nothing to do with that thermostat, or are you just cold?"

"I didn't touch it!" Nolan said. "I'm wearing two sweaters."

Layla crept to the hallway and watched the little dial on the wall. She had seen it set to seventy when the game started. Now it read sixty-two. She waited, arms crossed, until her cousin wandered out for water, glanced around, and cranked the dial down three more degrees.

"Gotcha," Layla said.

Her cousin froze with his hand still on the dial. "Your central heating," he said, with great dignity, "is a furnace with a dial. I was trying to cool the whole street."

"It's one house, and you've been doing it all afternoon." It had been vain of Layla to imagine some clever hidden cause, like a draft or a broken furnace, when the answer was a boy from a country where houses barely have thermostats at all. She turned the dial back up and marched him into the living room.

"Everything all right out there?" Ms. MacLeod called.

"Fine," Layla said. "He just learned a new word."

On the screen, the crowd stood up again, section by section, the wave rolling around and around the stadium, the Mexican wave, by any name a person chose to call it. Her cousin dropped onto the couch, and Nolan stood up alone in the middle of the room, arms raised, waiting.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: On the Holmes and Rahe stress scale, published in 1967, both changing residence and changing schools are listed as life events that require readjustment.
story:
Cameron counted the empty desks on his first morning at Kestrel Middle School and picked the one by the window, where at least he could watch the parking lot. His old school was two hundred miles away now, along with his best friend Frances, who had promised to text every day and had sent exactly one message about a sandwich. The new classroom smelled like floor cleaner, and the walls were so bare they looked arid, not a single poster anywhere.
