At lunch he sat with a kid named Gibson, who collected strawberry milk cartons and could burp the alphabet up to the letter J. Gibson was fine, but Cameron kept dropping his old jokes, the ones Frances already knew the endings to, and Gibson just stared at them like they were math homework. By Thursday, Cameron had a theory. He figured the problem was that Gibson was boring. To test it, he told the funniest story he had, the one about the goose that chased the mail carrier, using his best voices.

Gibson laughed so hard strawberry milk came out of his nose. So the problem was not Gibson. Cameron sat with that for a while, turning it over. If Gibson was funny, and the jokes were funny, then something else was broken. He wrote the possibilities on a napkin: Cameron is broken. School is broken. Town is broken.

On Friday Ms. Sánchez kept him after class. She slid a paper across her desk, a photocopy of a chart, and tapped one line. "Holmes and Rahe stress scale, published in 1967," she said. "Look what's on it." Cameron read down the list of life events. Changing residence was there. Changing schools was there too. Both of them, listed as events that required readjustment. He had done both in a single summer, back to back, like some kind of overachiever.

"You mean it's normal to feel like my jokes don't land?" he asked.

"I mean you moved house and moved schools, and both are on a list of things that take readjusting," she said. "It's not you. It's the math." Cameron folded the paper into his pocket and felt something loosen, the way a knot does when you finally find the right string. He wasn't broken, and neither was Gibson, and even the town might be off the hook.

At lunch he told Gibson the whole thing, and they made a game of it, giving Cameron's summer a score for maximum readjustment. Gibson awarded bonus points for the moving truck getting lost. Then Frances texted at last, asking if Cameron had made any friends yet, and Cameron took a photo of Gibson wearing a milk carton as a hat and sent it with one word: "Several."

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for the pharaoh Khufu about 4,500 years ago.
story:
Avery had to give a five-minute talk on ancient Egypt on Monday, and all she had was a half-read library book. On Saturday her mother dragged her to the war memorial downtown for a remembrance ceremony, and Avery brought the book along, figuring she could study while the speeches circulate through the crowd. She sat on the memorial steps between two granite lions and read the same paragraph three times. It said the Great Pyramid of Giza was built for the pharaoh Khufu about 4,500 years ago. The number refused to mean anything. It was too big.

Her grandmother was there, handing out paper programs near the flagpole. Avery counted on her fingers. Grandma was seventy-five. "How old are you?" she called across the grass. "Seventy-five, same as yesterday," Grandma said. Avery did the math on the back of a program. If every grandmother in history lived about seventy-five years, you could line up sixty grandmothers, hand to hand, and they would stretch all the way back to Khufu. Sixty. That was it. Sixty grandma-lifetimes.

"Who's Khufu?" said Adrian, dropping onto the step beside her with his own program rolled into a tube. "Pharaoh. His pyramid is the giant one at Giza," Avery said. "Built about 4,500 years ago." Adrian squinted at the memorial wall, where the oldest dates carved in the stone went back barely a hundred years. "So all this," he said, waving at the wall, "is like one slice of one grandma."

Then Avery noticed something. The Nile chapter said the river flooded every year and left mud that made the farming good, which was a factor in feeding all the pyramid workers. Flooding that helped. She had always assumed floods were bad, and here was a flood being useful. She tried flipping it around, an idea she tested out loud: if the flood came late one year, the mud would be thin, the crops would be poor, and a big building project would stall. Adrian nodded slowly. "So the pharaoh was basically waiting on a river."

The ceremony ended and people began to circulate back toward the parking lot. Grandma came over, spotted the program covered in numbers, and held it up. "Sixty of me, you said?" Avery nodded. Grandma laughed. "Then I'd better sit down somewhere and tell you about the year the river flooded my whole tomato patch."

activity: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
knowledge_domain: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
fact: To avoid feedback, microphones should not be pointed at the loudspeakers or held in front of them.
story:
Evan stood in the wings of the community theater, holding his microphone like it might bite. In the school concert's final number, he had one solo line, and he had been looking forward to this night for weeks. His costume crown, a cheap painted alloy that Ms. Bianchi had dug out of the props closet, slipped sideways every time he moved his head.

The chorus finished, and Evan stepped out. He walked toward the audience, straight at the tall loudspeaker at the front corner of the stage, and the microphone in his hand began to howl, a shriek that filled the whole theater. Kids in the front row covered their ears. Evan froze, his line vanished from his brain, and Ms. Bianchi waved frantically from the sound desk. The howl stopped as soon as he backed up a step.

"That was feedback," Loukas whispered from the wings when Evan retreated between verses. "Mira got it in rehearsal yesterday."

Evan's heart was pounding, but his brain had started working. Rehearsal, today, both times the mic had shrieked, and both times the person holding it had been down at that corner. He hypothesized that it wasn't the microphone itself, and it wasn't the singer. It was where the microphone was, near that speaker. If the mic got pointed at the loudspeaker, or held right in front of it, the howl came. Somewhere else on stage, nothing.

He had one chance to test it before his line came around again. The music swelled, and Evan moved forward, but this time he angled away from the corner, keeping the microphone turned out toward the middle of the house instead of at the speaker. No howl. Clear, warm silence from the sound system.

Evan sang his line, loud and steady, and the crown slid down over one eyebrow. He pushed it up with his free hand and grinned at Mira in the second row.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The word "propaganda" comes from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622.
story:
Ms. Huang had taped fake ads all over the history classroom walls, and Georgia's job was to find the tricks inside them. The sneaker poster shouted "Everyone's already wearing them!" while a soda ad showed a famous quarterback grinning over a can, and a poster for a cereal called the other cereals "mushy slop." Her notebook entries were supposed to dwindle down to a short list of techniques, but her list kept growing instead.

"Bandwagon," said Presley, jabbing the sneaker poster. "The quarterback one's a celebrity testimonial. Easy." Santino was copying the cereal ad's words in fancy letters: MUSHY SLOP. "Loaded words," he announced. "Somebody got paid to write that." Georgia wrote both answers down, then stopped. At the bottom of the wall hung a war poster with a stern Uncle pointing a finger, and under it Ms. Huang had written one word in red marker: propaganda. Something about the word bothered her, the way a pebble in a shoe bothers a foot. Persuasion was a trick, sure. But why did this word have its own special poster?

The dictionary app on the classroom tablet solved it. "It comes from a committee," Georgia said slowly, reading. "A Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith. The Congregatio de Propaganda Fide. Pope Gregory XV set it up in 1622." Santino's pen stopped mid-swoosh. "So a word for sneaky war posters started as church business?" "Not sneaky, exactly," Georgia said. "It just meant spreading ideas around. Somewhere it picked up the sneaky part." She wondered if that was fair. If everyone started using a word one way, did the old meaning just evaporate?

She tested her idea out loud. "Okay, if I said, 'Everyone in Rome joined the committee because everyone was doing it,' what technique is that?" Presley groaned. "Bandwagon. Even popes can't escape it." Georgia laughed so hard she snorted, and the noise made Ms. Huang look up from her desk with one eyebrow raised, like a cat who suspected an unguarded fish.

For her exit ticket, Georgia wrote: sneaker poster, bandwagon; cereal ad, loaded words; quarterback, testimonial; and at the bottom, the whole 1622 story with the Pope's name spelled carefully. Her supply of blank space was dwindling fast, so she squeezed the last line into the margin: "Despair is corrosive, said nobody on these posters, because ads only sell happy." Ms. Huang read it twice, then wrote one word beside it in red: "More?" Georgia grinned and flipped her paper over.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A ranking shows order but not distance: first and second place might differ by a hundredth of a second or by a whole minute.
story:
Gabriella set the table fast, because Dad had promised they could watch the finals replay during dinner, and the stream only stayed up until eight. She put the water glasses where the light from the ceiling lamp would refract through them, making little rainbows on the wood, because Mackenzie loved that and Mackenzie was coming over straight from her own swim practice, hungry and hoping.

"Second place," Mackenzie said, dropping into her chair and reaching for the bread before her coat was fully off. "That's what I need. Top two make the county squad, and rankings go up tomorrow morning at nine." She tore the bread in half and gave the bigger piece to Gabriella without seeming to notice she'd done it.

While Mom served the rice, Gabriella remembered last summer, when Mackenzie had missed the squad by one spot and cried in the equipment shed so nobody would see. Gabriella had sat outside the door and slid a frozen juice box under it, and neither of them had said anything about it, but Mackenzie had drunk it, because the empty box appeared later in the bin.

The race started on the laptop, propped against the salt shaker. Eight swimmers, and at the finish the screen froze the medalists in a row: gold, silver, bronze. The time beside the silver swimmer read 52.13, and the gold read 52.12. One hundredth of a second. Mackenzie laughed a short, unhappy laugh. "A hundredth. That's a blink. That's less than a blink." Her nervousness was infectious; even Gabriella started bouncing her foot under the table.

"It says nothing about how far apart they really were," Gabriella said slowly, watching the two numbers. "A ranking shows who beat who, but not by how much." She turned the laptop so Mackenzie could see the board from a district meet two seasons ago, where first and second had been separated by a whole minute, and both finishes still said 1st and 2nd, same as here.

"So the girl who got silver tonight," Mackenzie said, "could have lost by a hundredth or by a whole minute, and the ranking would look exactly the same."

"That's the component they leave out," Gabriella said. "The distance."

Dad carried in the chicken, and Mom shooed the laptop two inches sideways to make room. Mackenzie picked up her fork, then set it down again and pulled out her phone. "Can I text Liam? He keeps every heat sheet from regionals. If I'm sitting second by a hundredth, I want to know. If it's by a minute, I want to know that too."

Gabriella slid the phone across the table to her, screen already unlocked. "Tell him hurry," she said. "Dinner's getting cold, and eight o'clock is coming."

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Marble is a metamorphic rock formed when limestone is changed by heat and pressure.
story:
Kate slid three rocks across the planetarium's display table while the star projector hummed above them, throwing galaxies across the dome. Mr. Joshi had set out the challenge before the show: sort every rock as igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic, and the first team to get all eight right would pick the constellation for tonight's laser show.

Jayce slammed down a chunk of dark glassy rock. "Igneous. Volcano rock. Done. That's three." He wanted to beat the team from Mrs. Alvarez's class, and he wanted it badly, because last week they had beaten him at everything from rope climbing to spelling.

Kate picked up the last rock, smooth and cream-colored with faint swirls, and felt a flicker of despair. It didn't look like it had cooled from melted rock. It didn't look like squeezed-together layers of sand or shells, either. It looked like nothing, which was the worst thing a rock could look like. "The clues are about how they formed," she said slowly. "But you can't see how a rock formed. You have to infer it from what's in front of you." She turned the sample over, and on the bottom, almost hidden, was a tiny paper label from the museum's collection: marble.

"Marble's just fancy countertop stuff," Jayce said, reaching for the sorting tray. "I'd say igneous."

"Wait." Kate's eyes went to the plaque by the door, the one about the marble statue in the lobby. She had read it while waiting in line, mostly because Jayce was taking forever with his shoelace. The words came back to her now: seabed, limestone, heat, pressure. "That statue out front. The plaque says the marble started as limestone from an old seabed, and heat and pressure changed it into marble. Changed. That's metamorphic. Marble's metamorphic."

Jayce made a face. "You're telling me the lobby statue used to be a beach?"

"Basically."

He stared at the marble sample for a long second, then slid it out of the igneous tray and dropped it into the metamorphic one. "Okay, okay. But if we lose to Mrs. Alvarez's class because of a beach rock, I'm telling everyone it was your hypothetical idea."

Mr. Joshi checked the trays and raised an eyebrow at Kate. "So, team. Which constellation will it be?"

Jayce grinned. "Orion. The hunter. Named after a guy who got thrown into the sky." He pointed at the marble. "And he probably used to be a beach, too."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Airplane mode turns off a phone's radio signals, including the cellular connection it uses for calls and texts.
story:
Christopher held the small rectangle in both hands, the way his mother had handed it over that morning, like it was a bird that might startle. His first phone. The rules on the fridge read: homework first, screens off at eight, no phone at the table. He had agreed to all of them, and mostly he meant it, though he remembered the gradual way his old tablet rules had loosened last summer until nobody followed them at all. He didn't want that to happen here.

He typed a message to Ronald, who lived two floors down in the same building their landlord owned: "I got a phone. Send me something." Then he waited. Nothing came. He sent a test text to Mia, who had a phone already and always answered fast. Nothing came from her either. Christopher frowned at the bars at the top of the screen, or rather at the empty space where bars should be. He remembered flipping through the settings earlier, poking at every colorful switch just to see what it did. One of them had been on when he found it, and he had tapped it without reading the label.

He opened settings again and scrolled until he found the switch he suspected. Airplane mode, it said, and it was on. "Airplane mode," he said out loud, feeling a little foolish. "That's the one that turns off the phone's radio signals, including the cellular connection it uses for calls and texts." His cousin had complained about the exact same thing at Mia's birthday party, saying no messages were coming through, and everyone had laughed and nobody had fixed it. Christopher tapped the switch off. A message chimed, then another, then three more, stacked up like planes finally cleared to land.

The first was from his mother, sent hours ago: "Testing. Do you like it?" Then one from Ronald: "Movie in the courtyard at 7. Coming?" He had nearly missed both, all because of one switch he'd flipped out of curiosity. He typed "Coming" to Ronald, then added, "Guess what I just figured out." Downstairs at seven, the courtyard lights flickered on and Ronald was already saving him a chair. "So what did you figure out?" Ronald asked, holding out the popcorn.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In Judaism, shiva, from the Hebrew word for 'seven', is a seven-day period of mourning after a burial, when visitors come to comfort the family.
story:
The rain had begun to saturate everything, the windshield, the shoulders of Cole's jacket, the box of Grandma Ruth's favorite lemon cookies balanced on his knees. In the front seat, Dad drove with both hands on the wheel, quieter than usual, because Grandpa had been buried that morning and now they were driving to Grandma's apartment for the first night of visitors. Wallace and Nate sat squeezed in beside Cole, since their moms had agreed they could come along.

"Seven days of this," Dad said, glancing at the mirror. "It's called shiva. From the Hebrew word for seven."

"Seven whole days of people coming over?" Wallace asked. "That's a lot of casseroles."

Cole stared out at the smeared streetlights. His problem was simpler and bigger than casseroles. He had to say something to Grandma, and he had nothing. On a napkin in his pocket he had written an objective list of options, ranked: "Sorry about Grandpa," "He was funny," and "I liked his harmonica." Every one of them sounded wrong when he said it silently to himself. His eyes had been burning all day, and he remembered Mr. Li saying in science that tears involved hormones, which at least meant his body was doing it on its own and it wasn't something he was choosing to fail at.

Inside, the apartment smelled of coffee and onions and a little bit of damp wool, because so many coats had been dropped on the bed. Grandma sat in a low chair near the window with her shoes off, and people kept bending toward her, murmuring. Cole noticed something as he hung back by the door: nobody was saying anything clever. A woman in a gray scarf just sat beside Grandma and held her hand for ten whole minutes without talking. A man brought her tea she didn't drink, and she still nodded at him like it mattered.

So that was the rule, Cole thought. The visitors weren't there to fix anything, because nobody could. They were just there, filling up the room, so the mourning wasn't something Grandma had to do alone. Cole tested it right away. He crossed out his whole napkin list in his head, carried the lemon cookies over, and set them on the table beside her chair without a speech. Then he sat down on the carpet near her feet, because the good chair was taken.

"You're not going anywhere?" Grandma asked, looking down at him.

"Seven days," Cole said. "I can do day one."

Grandma reached over and put her hand on his head, the way she used to check him for a fever, and Wallace slid down onto the carpet on her other side and ate a cookie.

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Obsidian is volcanic glass: lava that cooled so quickly that crystals had no time to form.
story:
Wyatt crouched at the picnic table in his backyard, three shoeboxes in a row, each one labeled in marker: IGNEOUS, SEDIMENTARY, METAMORPHIC. He had to sort twelve rocks by tomorrow, and every single one looked like a rock.

"Start with what you know," Yousuf said, flipping through Wyatt's science notebook. "The granite goes in igneous. That's the one with the speckles."

"That's one down," Wyatt said. "Eleven to go."

Yousuf held up a chunk of sandstone. "This one's like glued-together sand, so sedimentary." He dropped it in the correct box, then reached for the last rock and went still. It was black and glossy, curved like a broken bottle, and its edge caught the sunlight. "Where did you even get this? Somebody smashed a bottle and it fossilized or something."

Wyatt's first instinct was to agree, because it looked exactly like glass. Then he remembered the museum field trip in October, when Derek had pressed his face to the same kind of shiny black stone in the geology hall and said, "This is just melted bottle bits, right?" A guide had been standing nearby, and she'd laughed and said, "That's obsidian. It's volcanic glass, lava that cooled so quickly that crystals had no time to form." Derek had written nothing down, but Wyatt had scribbled it on his ticket stub because it sounded like something Ms. Visser would put on a quiz.

"Wait," Wyatt said now, digging the stub out of his pencil case. The crumpled paper still held his handwriting. He read it out loud. "Obsidian. Volcanic glass. Lava cooled so fast that crystals never formed."

Yousuf turned the rock over twice, squinting. "So no crystals in there at all? Granite's got crystals all over it."

"Right. The granite cooled slow, deep underground. This cooled fast." Wyatt took it from him and held it beside the granite to demonstrate the difference, the speckled gray roughness next to the slick black face. "Which box?"

Yousuf grinned and tapped the igneous box. "Lava. Igneous."

Wyatt dropped it in with the granite, then picked up the two mystery rocks still left on the table and held them up against the afternoon light. "Last two," he said. "Look for crystals."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: A name a group uses for itself is called an endonym, and a name outsiders use for it is an exonym; Germans call their country Deutschland, while English speakers say Germany.
story:
The poster paper wrinkled every time Alexa tried to smooth it, and the glue stick was almost dead. Her project for the school heritage fair was due Friday, and she had one question she could not shake: the country her grandmother came from had two names, and Alexa had written the English one across the top in fat blue letters. It looked wrong now, like calling someone by a nickname they never chose. She smoothed the paper one more time and decided she needed real data.

At lunch she found Charlie in the cafeteria, dumping ketchup on everything. "Your cousin visited from Germany this summer, right?" Alexa asked. "Did she call it Germany?" Charlie laughed so hard he nearly knocked over his milk. "She kept saying Deutschland. When my dad kept saying Germany, she said, 'That's your word for it, not mine.'" Alexa pulled out her notebook. "So the people who live there use their own name, and we use a different one." She wrote both words down, side by side.

In Ms. Addo's class, Alexa raised her hand and told the class what she had figured out. "A name a group uses for itself is called an endonym," she said, "and a name outsiders use for it is an exonym. Deutschland versus Germany." Aaden, who sat by the window and rarely spoke, put his hand up halfway. "My family says Côte d'Ivoire, but a lot of maps say Ivory Coast." His voice got stronger as he went on. "I always thought the map name was the real one." Ms. Addo smiled but said nothing, which was her way of letting students keep the discovery.

Alexa wanted to test whether the pattern held for everyone, not just two people, so she made a survey on notebook paper and stood by the gym door after practice, asking students and the coach what their families called the places they came from. She wrote down nine answers. Eight fit. The ninth kid shrugged and said, "Same thing, whatever," which Alexa decided was fine, since one exception did not sink a whole pattern, though she admitted to herself that a survey of nine had a high probability of being wrong about a school of four hundred. Charlie helped her tally the answers even though he kept asking whether this counted as homework he could copy. "You can't copy thinking," she told him, and he grinned and kept counting anyway.

Aaden wanted something too: he wanted the fair's world map to show the names families actually used. So on Thursday, Alexa and Aaden stayed late with Ms. Addo's permission, writing small labels in marker and pinning them beside the printed ones. It was not trivial work; holding the labels steady while the tape fought them sustained them long past the point where their arms ached.

On Friday, Aaden's grandmother stopped at the map, touched the label beside Côte d'Ivoire, and said something to him in a language Alexa did not know. Aaden translated it, glowing. "She says it looks like home wrote its own name on the map."

activity: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points
knowledge_domain: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points
fact: Horizontal edges above your eye level slope down toward the vanishing points, while edges below your eye level slope up toward them.
story:
Antoine sat on the floor of his grandfather's living room with a pencil, a ruler, and a blank page, trying to draw the room the way the art book said: two vanishing points, one at each end of the horizon line. His friend Kalen sat beside him, holding the book open on his knees. Grandpa had gone to accommodate his afternoon nap, so they had the room to themselves except for the cat, who watched them from the armchair like a nocturnal creature who had given up on sleeping in the daytime.

Antoine drew the back wall first, then the lines for the floor, and they worked. The floor looked like a floor. But the ceiling was a disaster. He had sloped the ceiling edges upward toward the vanishing points, because a ceiling is high, so it should go up, and now the whole thing looked like the ceiling was floating away from the house, drifting off the page.

"It looks like Grandpa's ceiling is escaping," Kalen said, holding the drawing up next to the actual room. Antoine stared from the paper to the real ceiling and back. The ceiling was above his eye level, that was true. But then he looked down at the floor lines, the ones that looked right, and noticed something: the floor was below his eye level, and those lines sloped upward toward the vanishing points. He tested a simple idea. He drew two fresh lines for the ceiling, but sloped them downward toward the vanishing points instead.

"There," he said. The ceiling settled onto the walls like it belonged there. "Above your eye level, the lines go down to the vanishing points. Below it, they go up." Kalen copied the trick onto his own page, and when Grandpa shuffled in later to brew the coffee he consumed like a dedicated consumer, cup after cup, he stopped behind them. "That's my room," he said, tapping the drawing. "You even got my chair in the corner." Antoine handed him the pencil. "Show us where your cat likes to sit," Kalen said.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: Fresh fruits and vegetables are often cheapest at the peak of their local harvest season, when farmers have the most to sell.
story:
Jayden pushed the cart down the produce aisle, and its wheels seemed to accelerate on the polished floor until his mom called him back. He stopped in front of the strawberries. Two weeks ago, one pint had cost four dollars, and he had walked away with nothing. Today the sign said two dollars. That made no sense. Strawberries were strawberries. He had even suspected the store of punishing him for not buying sooner.

"Everything okay back there?" his mom asked. She was comparing two bags of flour, whose price had stayed stable for as long as Jayden could remember, which somehow made the strawberries stranger.

Ms. Shapiro from next door rolled her cart up beside him, hunting through the berry containers. "Perfect timing," she said. "Strawberries at the farmers' market cost half what they did a month earlier. This is when they're cheapest, at the peak of the local harvest season, because the farmers have the most to sell." She dropped four pints into her cart without even checking for bruises.

Jayden turned that over while he helped his mom pick out lettuce. A month ago the farmers must have had almost nothing to sell, and the price had been high. Now they had a lot, and the price was low. Nobody had raised or lowered anything out of meanness. There was a hidden rule underneath the price tags, a concept he couldn't see directly, like wind you only notice because the branches move. He wanted to test it. If lots of something made it cheap, then the tomatoes at the back of the store, stacked in a huge pyramid, should cost less than the lonely little basket of figs nearby. He walked over. Tomatoes, one fifty. Figs, six dollars. The pattern held.

At home he wrote a note to his friend Kristen, who was stuck home with a sprained ankle and had missed the whole trip.

Kristen, he wrote, you were right that I should stop blaming the grocery store. I changed my mind. The price isn't about us at all. Strawberries are half the price they were a month ago because it's the peak of the local harvest season and the farmers have the most to sell right now. I checked tomatoes against figs too. Long story. Saving you a smoothie. Jayden.

He taped the note to the pint he set aside for her and slid it into the freezer bag with the frozen bananas. Then he counted the rest of the berries, took out the blender, and pressed the button marked ice crush.
